title: The August Morning Bertha Benz Drove the Motor Car to Pforzheim
dek: In 1888, with buyers still unconvinced, the woman whose dowry had financed Carl Benz's work took his car on its first long journey without telling him.

story.event: Bertha Benz's first long-distance drive in the Benz Patent Motor Car, Mannheim to Pforzheim
story.summary: On 5 August 1888 Bertha Benz, whose dowry had helped finance Carl Benz's business, drove an improved Benz Patent Motor Car from Mannheim to Pforzheim with her sons Eugen and Richard, without her husband's knowledge, in the first long-distance journey by motor car. She bought fuel at a pharmacy in Wiesloch and made running repairs on the way. Her suggestion of an extra gear for hills was adopted, the car was exhibited in Munich and Paris, and Benz & Cie. became the world's largest car maker by 1900.
paragraphs: Before dawn on 5 August 1888, Bertha Benz left Mannheim in the newest version of her husband's motor car, the Patent Motor Car No. 3, with her teenage sons Eugen and Richard. Carl Benz did not know. They were going to see her mother in Pforzheim, Bertha's home town, roughly 100 kilometres away. No motor car had yet made a journey that long.

Some of the money in that car was hers. Born into a well-off Pforzheim family, Bertha Ringer had her dowry paid out in advance and invested it in Carl's small business, and for years the household lived close to the breadline while everything went into his work. By 1888 that work seemed stalled. Carl had applied for a patent on his vehicle in January 1886 and driven it in public that July; the local press reported it, but the hoped-for interest never came, and the horseless carriage was not thought practical. The German patent office's history calls him self-doubting and says he would never have allowed the trip.

The road tested everything. The company archive calls the circumstances legendary, and the accounts it and the museums tell agree on the outline. At Wiesloch she bought ligroin, a cleaning solvent the engine ran on, at the town pharmacy. She cleared a blocked fuel line with her hatpin and fixed the ignition with her garter. A blacksmith helped mend the chain, a cobbler nailed leather onto the wooden brake blocks, and on climbs they had to get out and push. Along the way they sent Carl telegrams.

The journey showed, in the Mercedes-Benz archive's words, the practicality of the motor vehicle, and the patent office says it gave Carl back his belief in the invention. It also changed the car: Bertha proposed another gear for hills, and he added it. That year the car was shown at an exhibition in Munich, and in 1889 at the World Exhibition in Paris. By 1900 Benz & Cie. was the largest car maker in the world. Carl later recalled that she "was more daring than me and undertook a journey that was decisive for the further development of the motor car."

quote.text: For in counsel, it is good to see dangers; and in execution, not to see them, except they be very great.
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon distrusted boldness as an adviser but valued it in the doing. The Benz story splits the work much as he suggests: Carl's doubts belonged to the workshop, while the road to Pforzheim needed someone who would not stop for every danger, only the large ones.

reflection: The car Bertha took was already patented and already running. What it lacked was a day on ordinary roads, with hills and no workshop nearby, and someone willing to find out what would break. Most of what went wrong was small and could be mended with what she carried, and each repair told Carl something the workshop had not.

You may have a piece of work that is ready in every way except that nobody has used it far from your desk. Bacon would say keep your caution for the planning, and leave most of it at home for the trip.
invitation: Choose one thing you have made that has only been tried in safe conditions. Ask one person to use it today somewhere ordinary, and write down the first thing that goes wrong.

research_notes: Credit: Bertha is named as co-founder because her dowry financed Carl's business from its earliest years (DPMA: dowry paid out in advance and invested in his small company; Mercedes-Benz Classic: her dowry saved the first company; Qatar Museums: co-investor from the outset). No loading source documents her formal legal status in Benz & Cie., so the story speaks of her money and does not call her a registered partner. Funding is recorded as mixed: the family's money carried Carl's work, but Benz & Cie. (founded in 1883) also had business partners, which the story does not discuss. Distance: DPMA says around 100 km to Pforzheim; the National Motor Museum and Qatar Museums say 106 km one way; Mercedes-Benz gives 180 km with the return and the signed memorial route is 194 km; the story says roughly 100 km one way. Sons' ages: Mercedes-Benz says 15 and 14, DPMA 15 and 13 (by the usual birth years, 1873 and 1874, the younger boy may have been 13 or 14); the story says 'teenage sons'. Duration: DPMA's 'almost 13-hour journey' is ambiguous about whether it includes the return, so no duration is given. Several road details (hatpin, garter, blacksmith, cobbler) are described by the Mercedes-Benz archive as legendary; the story says so and keeps only the details that DPMA, the National Motor Museum and Qatar Museums agree on; the National Motor Museum's account of a note left for Carl and a telegram asking for the chains appears in only one source and is left out. The Munich gold medal appears only in the Qatar Museums account and is omitted. Carl's 'more daring than me' line is an English rendering of his memoir (Lebensfahrt eines deutschen Erfinders, 1925) as quoted identically by DPMA and Qatar Museums; the memoir itself was not found online. Spelling: Mercedes-Benz and DPMA use Carl, the National Motor Museum Karl; Carl is used.
